references.title: Casual conditional vs formal inverted conditional
references.text:
Title: Casual conditional vs formal inverted conditional
When to use: Use only for an explicit inverted-conditional task; ordinary if conditionals remain valid.

Explanation: Conditional inversion can replace if with should, were, or had. Keep the condition type and time reference: should plus base verb, were to for a hypothetical action, and had plus past participle for a past counterfactual. Inversion changes register and can affect perceived likelihood.

Examples:
- If you should need a receipt, ask me. -> Should you need a receipt, ask me.
- If the system were to fail, we would stop. -> Were the system to fail, we would stop.
- If I had known, I would have called. -> Had I known, I would have called.

Boundary (incorrect example; do not imitate):
Bad: If should you need help, call. Do not retain if in the inverted form.
Why incorrect: Inverted conditional syntax replaces if rather than adding inversion after it.

Tags: formal_register, sentence_transformation, transformation, sentence, work, academic, conditional

references.title: Conversational phrase vs formal phrase
references.text:
Title: Conversational phrase vs formal phrase
When to use: Use for an everyday short expression when the request is about tone rather than a specialized term.

Explanation: Restate a conversational phrase in neutral language while preserving its speech act: request, apology, promise, or statement. Do not turn a suggestion into a command or add a deadline to a promise.

Examples:
- I don't understand that. -> I do not understand that point.
- I'll reply later. -> I will respond later.
- Sorry, that was my mistake. -> I apologize for my mistake.
- Let's talk about this later. -> I suggest we revisit this matter at a later time.

Boundary (incorrect example; do not imitate):
Original: I will reply. Bad rewrite: I will reply immediately. The time commitment was added.
Why incorrect: Adding immediately creates a new time commitment.

Tags: phrase_idiom, formal_register, translation, phrase, work, daily

references.title: Everyday wording vs formal wording
references.text:
Title: Everyday wording vs formal wording
When to use: Choose this for a local word-level register change. Use the sentence or phrase note when restructuring the whole utterance.

Explanation: Choose wording for the audience and purpose. A formal alternative can change tone without being more accurate. Preserve the original claim, certainty, and politeness; a grammatical informal sentence is not automatically wrong.

Examples:
- Please [get] written consent. -> Please obtain written consent.
- Could you [help] with the survey? -> Could you assist with the survey?
- We will [ask for] permission. -> We will request permission.
- We need to [get] approval first. -> We need to obtain approval first.

Boundary (incorrect example; do not imitate):
Original: We might finish today. Bad rewrite: We will finish today. The rewrite removes uncertainty.
Why incorrect: Keep the modal might; the source does not promise completion.

Tags: formal_register, advanced_synonym_precision, substitution, sentence, daily, work

references.title: Casual sentence vs formal rewrite
references.text:
Title: Casual sentence vs formal rewrite
When to use: Use for a whole-sentence register change without a more specific domain or grammatical target.

Explanation: Rewrite the sentence in a neutral professional tone while keeping its propositions intact. Do not add evidence, deadlines, magnitude, or completed actions. Formality does not require passive voice or abstract nouns.

Examples:
- We can't attend because we're busy. -> We cannot attend because we are busy.
- They messed up the schedule. -> They made errors in the schedule.
- We added a search option. -> We implemented a search option.
- I think you should probably reconsider this. -> I would recommend reconsidering this course of action.

Boundary (incorrect example; do not imitate):
Original: We added a feature. Bad rewrite: We deployed a feature. Implementation does not establish deployment.
Why incorrect: Adding a feature does not establish that it was released to users.

Tags: formal_register, sentence_transformation, transformation, sentence, work, daily, rewrite

references.title: Common everyday word vs advanced precise synonym
references.text:
Title: Common everyday word vs advanced precise synonym
When to use: Use for standalone vocabulary and sense restrictions; prefer a more specific note when a structural or domain objective is explicit.

Explanation: Word choice depends on sense, grammatical frame, and collocation. Context-free synonym cards practice possible associations, not universal substitutions. Insert a proposed answer into a sentence before claiming it is equivalent.

Examples:
- begin a procedure -> start a procedure
- finish a meeting -> conclude a meeting
- change part of a document -> modify part of a document
- start (verb) -> initiate

Boundary (incorrect example; do not imitate):
Original: A fast runner. Bad rewrite: An expeditious runner. The adjective does not fit that ordinary collocation.
Why incorrect: Choose an adjective that collocates with the intended noun and sense.

Tags: advanced_synonym_precision, topic_specific_vocab, substitution, sentence, daily, education, academic, vocab

references.title: Everyday health language vs formal medical language
references.text:
Title: Everyday health language vs formal medical language
When to use: Use for tone in symptom descriptions; this note does not diagnose conditions or recommend care.

Explanation: Preserve the symptom and the speaker in a health-related rewrite. Plain symptom descriptions can already be appropriate. Do not convert everyday uncertainty into a diagnosis or substitute a related medical condition.

Examples:
- I have a very bad headache. -> I have a severe headache.
- She is tired all the time. -> She experiences persistent tiredness.
- My stomach hurts. -> I have stomach pain.
- She's really tired all the time. -> She experiences persistent fatigue.

Boundary (incorrect example; do not imitate):
Original: I feel dizzy. Bad rewrite: I have vertigo. A general symptom does not establish that specific condition.
Why incorrect: Keep the stated symptom; the source does not establish a specific condition.

Tags: formal_register, sentence_transformation, transformation, sentence, health, rewrite

references.title: Informal health phrase vs formal medical phrase
references.text:
Title: Informal health phrase vs formal medical phrase
When to use: Use for short symptom expressions; not treatment, emergency triage, or symptom interpretation.

Explanation: Use a clear equivalent for the whole health-related phrase without making a diagnosis. Preserve who reports the experience. A reference for language should not imply clinical authority.

Examples:
- I feel sick to my stomach. -> I feel nauseated.
- I do not feel well. -> I feel unwell.
- My head hurts. -> I have a headache.
- I feel sick to my stomach. -> I am experiencing nausea.

Boundary (incorrect example; do not imitate):
Original: I feel unwell. Bad rewrite: I have an infection. The diagnosis is unsupported.
Why incorrect: Feeling unwell is not evidence for a specific diagnosis.

Tags: phrase_idiom, formal_register, translation, phrase, health

references.title: Everyday money word vs precise financial term
references.text:
Title: Everyday money word vs precise financial term
When to use: Use for a defined financial vocabulary task; this note is not a complete accounting reference or financial advice.

Explanation: Financial labels require a specified meaning. A broad category and one example of it are not interchangeable in every sentence. Where the prompt is underspecified, explain the missing distinction instead of supplying artificial certainty.

Examples:
- spend less money -> reduce spending
- recover money previously lost -> recoup the money
- an increase in the price -> a price increase
- money earned from sales before expenses (noun) -> revenue

Boundary (incorrect example; do not imitate):
Original: Money was received. Bad rewrite: A profit was earned. Receipts alone do not establish a profit.
Why incorrect: Receipts alone do not establish that revenue exceeded relevant costs.

Tags: advanced_synonym_precision, topic_specific_vocab, substitution, sentence, money, finance, vocab

references.title: Verb phrase vs nominalized form
references.text:
Title: Verb phrase vs nominalized form
When to use: Use for an explicit verb-to-noun transformation, not as a synonym for passive voice.

Explanation: Nominalization expresses an action through a noun, such as approval or revision. It can help discuss a process as a topic, but often adds words or hides the actor. Preserve the actor when it matters; a noun-based version is not automatically better writing.

Examples:
- The board approved the plan. -> The board gave approval to the plan.
- We revised the schedule. -> We made a revision to the schedule.
- They investigated the error. -> They conducted an investigation into the error.

Boundary (incorrect example; do not imitate):
Original: The board approved it. Bad rewrite: Approval occurred. Responsibility is lost.
Why incorrect: Nominalization should retain the responsible actor when that actor matters.

Tags: formal_register, sentence_transformation, transformation, sentence, work, academic, nominalization

references.title: Two sentences vs non-restrictive relative clause
references.text:
Title: Two sentences vs non-restrictive relative clause
When to use: Use when extra information is parenthetical, not necessary to identify the noun.

Explanation: A non-defining relative clause adds parenthetical information about an already identified referent. Separate an inserted clause with two commas and keep a relative pronoun such as who or which; do not use that. Contrast this with a defining clause that selects a referent.

Examples:
- Asha lives in Leeds. She designed this logo. -> Asha, who designed this logo, lives in Leeds.
- This single invoice is overdue. It arrived on Friday. -> This invoice, which arrived on Friday, is overdue.
- Our only office has reopened. It closed in May. -> Our only office, which closed in May, has reopened.

Boundary (incorrect example; do not imitate):
Bad: Asha, that designed the logo, lives in Leeds. Use who, not that, in this parenthetical clause.
Why incorrect: Parenthetical relative clauses do not allow that as their relative pronoun.

Tags: sentence_transformation, complex_sentence_combination, relative_clause, non_restrictive, transformation, sentence, daily

references.title: Two clauses vs participle clause
references.text:
Title: Two clauses vs participle clause
When to use: Use when combining clauses with a participle opener. Do not use for noun-identifying relative clauses.

Explanation: An introductory participle clause normally shares its understood subject with the main clause. Having plus a past participle marks an earlier completed action; an -ing clause may describe simultaneous activity. Check subject and time relations before combining sentences.

Examples:
- Nora checked the address. Then she mailed the form. -> Having checked the address, Nora mailed the form.
- Omar walked home. He listened to a podcast as he walked. -> Walking home, Omar listened to a podcast.
- The students finished the task. Then they left. -> Having finished the task, the students left.
- She studied the data. She reached a conclusion. -> Having studied the data, she reached a conclusion.

Boundary (incorrect example; do not imitate):
Bad: Walking to the office, the rain soaked me. The grammatical subject would be the rain, not the walker.
Why incorrect: The introductory clause needs the walker as the main clause subject.

Tags: sentence_transformation, complex_sentence_combination, participle_clause, transformation, sentence, daily

references.title: Active voice vs passive voice
references.text:
Title: Active voice vs passive voice
When to use: Use for an explicit active/passive transformation, not a general demand to sound formal.

Explanation: For an ordinary transitive clause, passive be plus a past participle makes the object the subject. Preserve tense, participants, and negation. Choose voice for focus; the passive agent may be omitted when unknown or unneeded, but do not invent an agent when converting back.

Examples:
- Mira checked the invoice. -> The invoice was checked by Mira.
- The parcel was packed by Leo. -> Leo packed the parcel.
- They have not approved the plan. -> The plan has not been approved by them.
- The committee reviewed the proposal. -> The proposal was reviewed by the committee.

Boundary (incorrect example; do not imitate):
Original: Someone opened the door. Bad rewrite: The manager opened the door. The manager was not identified.
Why incorrect: An unspecified agent cannot be replaced with an invented manager.

Tags: sentence_transformation, passive_voice, active_voice, transformation, sentence, work, daily

references.title: Vague adjective vs precise adjective
references.text:
Title: Vague adjective vs precise adjective
When to use: Use for contextual adjective substitutions; a request for formality alone does not establish a new quality.

Explanation: An adjective describes a particular dimension: size, severity, clarity, or importance. Choose the intended dimension from the context rather than replacing every vague adjective with a stronger one.

Examples:
- The instructions are [easy to understand]. -> The instructions are clear.
- The timetable is [not clear]. -> The timetable is unclear.
- The error is [very serious]. -> The error is severe.
- The plan has a [bad] flaw. -> The plan has a critical flaw.

Boundary (incorrect example; do not imitate):
Original: A large building. Bad rewrite: An important building. Size and importance are different dimensions.
Why incorrect: A physical size adjective cannot be replaced with an importance judgment.

Tags: advanced_synonym_precision, substitution, sentence, daily, work, sport

references.title: General wording vs precise synonym
references.text:
Title: General wording vs precise synonym
When to use: Use for a contextual word substitution without a special grammatical transformation; check the whole sentence after inserting the answer.

Explanation: A replacement must fit the word sense, grammar, and surrounding words. Similar dictionary meanings do not guarantee interchangeability. A longer alternative such as utilize is not inherently more precise than use.

Examples:
- The diagram [shows] the process. -> The diagram illustrates the process.
- Please [look at closely] the signature. -> Please examine the signature.
- The meeting will [start] at noon. -> The meeting will begin at noon.
- The project was very [big]. -> The project was very substantial.

Boundary (incorrect example; do not imitate):
Original: She asked a question. Bad rewrite: She solicited a question. The object relationship changes.
Why incorrect: Asking a question and requesting that someone supply a question are different acts.

Tags: advanced_synonym_precision, substitution, sentence, daily, work

references.title: Two sentences vs relative clause
references.text:
Title: Two sentences vs relative clause
When to use: Use when extra information selects one referent from several, or the card explicitly requests a defining relative clause.

Explanation: A defining relative clause identifies which person or thing is intended. It normally has no surrounding commas. Use who for people and which or that for things; preserve the noun reference. Choosing defining rather than non-defining changes the information structure.

Examples:
- Several analysts applied. The analyst who speaks Arabic was selected. -> The selected analyst is identified by the clause who speaks Arabic.
- Choose the file. It contains the final figures. -> Choose the file that contains the final figures.
- I need the tool. It opens this panel. -> I need the tool that opens this panel.
- The manager approved the budget. She leads the project. -> The manager who leads the project approved the budget.

Boundary (incorrect example; do not imitate):
If there is only one already identified sister, adding identifying information without commas may imply a different context.
Why incorrect: Defining and parenthetical clauses assume different identification contexts.

Tags: sentence_transformation, complex_sentence_combination, relative_clause, transformation, sentence, daily

references.title: Casual observation vs formal scientific description
references.text:
Title: Casual observation vs formal scientific description
When to use: Use for experimental observations and research reports, not for a general request to define a scientific term.

Explanation: Report observations and interpretations separately. A rewrite must not invent statistical tests, significance, mechanisms, or support for a hypothesis. Active voice and first person may be appropriate; follow the relevant publication or course convention.

Examples:
- We noticed an unexpected change. -> We observed an unexpected change.
- The test ran as planned. -> The test proceeded as planned.
- We do not know why the signal changed. -> The reason for the signal change remains unknown.
- The experiment worked. -> The experiment functioned as intended.

Boundary (incorrect example; do not imitate):
Original: Scores improved. Bad rewrite: Scores improved significantly. Statistical significance was not established.
Why incorrect: Do not imply a statistical result without a stated test and evidence.

Tags: formal_register, sentence_transformation, transformation, sentence, science, academic, rewrite

references.title: Loose phrase vs single precise verb
references.text:
Title: Loose phrase vs single precise verb
When to use: Use when a card explicitly requests a single verb, before applying generic synonym or register guidance.

Explanation: Replace a phrase with one verb only when it expresses the same action and takes compatible objects and prepositions. Preserve tense and agent. Concision does not license inventing successful outcomes.

Examples:
- They [talked about] the timetable. -> They discussed the timetable.
- She [made improvements to] the draft. -> She improved the draft.
- We [gave an explanation of] the rule. -> We explained the rule.
- He [talked about] the risks at length. -> He addressed the risks at length.

Boundary (incorrect example; do not imitate):
Original: They tried to repair it. Bad rewrite: They repaired it. Attempt and success are different.
Why incorrect: A repair attempt does not imply a successful repair.

Tags: single_precise_verb, advanced_synonym_precision, substitution, sentence, work, sport, tech, daily

references.title: Casual sport report vs formal sport reporting language
references.text:
Title: Casual sport report vs formal sport reporting language
When to use: Use for full sentences about sporting performance rather than short predictions or sport terminology.

Explanation: Report an athletic performance with the same level of detail and certainty as the source. Clear journalistic prose need not add composure, teamwork, or records when they were not described.

Examples:
- She played very well under pressure. -> She performed very well under pressure.
- The team won by three points. -> The team secured a three-point victory.
- The players made several mistakes. -> The players made several errors.
- She played really well under pressure. -> She performed very well under pressure.

Boundary (incorrect example; do not imitate):
Original: The player performed well. Bad rewrite: The player broke the league record. The achievement is unsupported.
Why incorrect: A record requires comparison evidence, not a general positive assessment.

Tags: formal_register, sentence_transformation, transformation, sentence, sport, rewrite

references.title: Informal sport phrase vs formal sports commentary phrase
references.text:
Title: Informal sport phrase vs formal sports commentary phrase
When to use: Use for phrase-level sport reporting; use sport sentence guidance for a full performance description.

Explanation: Rephrase a short sporting expression while retaining the prediction, result, and confidence level. A professional report need not exaggerate athletic performance.

Examples:
- They may win. -> Victory is possible for them.
- They are likely to lose. -> They are expected to lose.
- The match is over. -> The match has ended.
- They're going to lose. -> They are expected to lose.

Boundary (incorrect example; do not imitate):
Original: They may win. Bad rewrite: They will win. A possibility became a certainty.
Why incorrect: May expresses possibility; will asserts a predicted outcome more strongly.

Tags: phrase_idiom, formal_register, translation, phrase, sport

references.title: Generic sport description vs precise sports term
references.text:
Title: Generic sport description vs precise sports term
When to use: Use for contextual sport vocabulary, not an unsupported claim about a score or achievement.

Explanation: Choose a sporting expression only when its meaning is supplied by the task. Admission of defeat, loss of a match, and conceding a goal are different events. Do not infer a record from a general description of good performance.

Examples:
- a session for practicing a sport -> a training session
- admit defeat in a contest -> concede defeat
- the points recorded for each side -> the score
- win (verb) -> triumph

Boundary (incorrect example; do not imitate):
Original: The runner did well. Bad rewrite: The runner set a personal best. No record comparison was given.
Why incorrect: Good performance does not establish a personal record.

Tags: advanced_synonym_precision, topic_specific_vocab, substitution, sentence, sport, vocab

references.title: Generic description vs precise technical term
references.text:
Title: Generic description vs precise technical term
When to use: Use for software-operation vocabulary with enough context; do not infer a root cause from an outage.

Explanation: Use technical terms according to the described operation. Testing, reviewing, deploying, and optimizing are not interchangeable improvements in formality. Preserve whether the source states an action, outcome, or symptom.

Examples:
- The process stopped unexpectedly. -> The process terminated unexpectedly.
- We need to fix the defect. -> We need to resolve the defect.
- Make execution faster. -> Improve execution speed.
- The app [crashed]. -> The app terminated unexpectedly.

Boundary (incorrect example; do not imitate):
Original: The program was implemented. Bad rewrite: The program was deployed. Implementation does not entail release.
Why incorrect: Building software and releasing it are different lifecycle events.

Tags: advanced_synonym_precision, topic_specific_vocab, substitution, sentence, tech, vocab

references.title: Casual workplace language vs formal business language
references.text:
Title: Casual workplace language vs formal business language
When to use: Use for workplace sentence rewrites such as target reports and email openings; use the phrase note for short interaction formulas.

Explanation: For workplace reports, make the actor, action, and limits of the claim clear. Choose professional wording without implying that all business writing must be impersonal. Retain hedging where the speaker is uncertain.

Examples:
- We did not hit the target. -> We did not meet the target.
- I am checking on the request. -> I am following up on the request.
- She runs the branch. -> She manages the branch.
- We didn't hit our targets this quarter. -> We did not meet our targets this quarter.

Boundary (incorrect example; do not imitate):
Original: We think the delay is temporary. Bad rewrite: The delay is temporary. The confidence changed.
Why incorrect: Removing we think strengthens the level of certainty.

Tags: formal_register, sentence_transformation, transformation, sentence, work, rewrite

references.title: Informal work phrase vs formal workplace alternative
references.text:
Title: Informal work phrase vs formal workplace alternative
When to use: Use for short workplace interaction phrases; use the workplace sentence note for reports of organizational facts.

Explanation: Preserve the intent of workplace interaction: follow up, request a response, close a meeting, or acknowledge an idea. Politeness does not require a long formula. Keep urgency only when originally stated.

Examples:
- Let us finish the meeting. -> Let us bring the meeting to a close.
- Please reply about the schedule. -> Please respond regarding the schedule.
- That is a useful suggestion. -> That is a useful proposal.
- That's a great idea. -> That is an excellent idea.

Boundary (incorrect example; do not imitate):
Original: Please reply when you can. Bad rewrite: Respond today. The deadline and politeness changed.
Why incorrect: Preserve the flexible timing and the original request tone.

Tags: phrase_idiom, formal_register, translation, phrase, work

references.title: Everyday work word vs precise business term
references.text:
Title: Everyday work word vs precise business term
When to use: Use for workplace vocabulary with a defined action or purpose, not general email tone.

Explanation: Professional terms may name different activities rather than stronger synonyms. A consultation seeks advice; not every meeting does. State the context needed for the target term and preserve participants.

Examples:
- work together on a task -> collaborate on a task
- a meeting to seek advice -> a consultation
- leave a project voluntarily -> withdraw from a project
- meeting to seek professional advice (noun) -> consultation

Boundary (incorrect example; do not imitate):
Original: A meeting occurred. Bad rewrite: A consultation occurred. The purpose of the meeting was not stated.
Why incorrect: A consultation implies an advice-seeking purpose absent from a generic meeting.

Tags: advanced_synonym_precision, topic_specific_vocab, substitution, sentence, work, vocab

When to use: Use only for an explicit inverted-conditional task; ordinary if conditionals remain valid.

Why incorrect: Inverted conditional syntax replaces if rather than adding inversion after it.

Tags: formal_register, sentence_transformation, transformation, sentence, work, academic, conditional"}, {"id": "en_formal_phrase_rephrasing", "title": "Conversational phrase vs formal phrase", "text": "Title: Conversational phrase vs formal phrase
When to use: Use for an everyday short expression when the request is about tone rather than a specialized term.

Explanation: Restate a conversational phrase in neutral language while preserving its speech act: request, apology, promise, or statement. Do not turn a suggestion into a command or add a deadline to a promise.

Examples:
- I don't understand that. -> I do not understand that point.
- I'll reply later. -> I will respond later.
- Sorry, that was my mistake. -> I apologize for my mistake.
- Let's talk about this later. -> I suggest we revisit this matter at a later time.

Boundary (incorrect example; do not imitate):
Original: I will reply. Bad rewrite: I will reply immediately. The time commitment was added.
Why incorrect: Adding immediately creates a new time commitment.

Tags: phrase_idiom, formal_register, translation, phrase, work, daily"}, {"id": "en_formal_register_precision", "title": "Everyday wording vs formal wording", "text": "Title: Everyday wording vs formal wording
When to use: Choose this for a local word-level register change. Use the sentence or phrase note when restructuring the whole utterance.

Explanation: Choose wording for the audience and purpose. A formal alternative can change tone without being more accurate. Preserve the original claim, certainty, and politeness; a grammatical informal sentence is not automatically wrong.

Examples:
- Please [get] written consent. -> Please obtain written consent.
- Could you [help] with the survey? -> Could you assist with the survey?
- We will [ask for] permission. -> We will request permission.
- We need to [get] approval first. -> We need to obtain approval first.

Boundary (incorrect example; do not imitate):
Original: We might finish today. Bad rewrite: We will finish today. The rewrite removes uncertainty.
Why incorrect: Keep the modal might; the source does not promise completion.

Tags: formal_register, advanced_synonym_precision, substitution, sentence, daily, work"}, {"id": "en_formal_rewrite_sentence", "title": "Casual sentence vs formal rewrite", "text": "Title: Casual sentence vs formal rewrite
When to use: Use for a whole-sentence register change without a more specific domain or grammatical target.

Explanation: Rewrite the sentence in a neutral professional tone while keeping its propositions intact. Do not add evidence, deadlines, magnitude, or completed actions. Formality does not require passive voice or abstract nouns.

Examples:
- We can't attend because we're busy. -> We cannot attend because we are busy.
- They messed up the schedule. -> They made errors in the schedule.
- We added a search option. -> We implemented a search option.
- I think you should probably reconsider this. -> I would recommend reconsidering this course of action.

Boundary (incorrect example; do not imitate):
Original: We added a feature. Bad rewrite: We deployed a feature. Implementation does not establish deployment.
Why incorrect: Adding a feature does not establish that it was released to users.

Tags: formal_register, sentence_transformation, transformation, sentence, work, daily, rewrite"}, {"id": "en_general_vocabulary_precision", "title": "Common everyday word vs advanced precise synonym", "text": "Title: Common everyday word vs advanced precise synonym
When to use: Use for standalone vocabulary and sense restrictions; prefer a more specific note when a structural or domain objective is explicit.

Explanation: Word choice depends on sense, grammatical frame, and collocation. Context-free synonym cards practice possible associations, not universal substitutions. Insert a proposed answer into a sentence before claiming it is equivalent.

Examples:
- begin a procedure -> start a procedure
- finish a meeting -> conclude a meeting
- change part of a document -> modify part of a document
- start (verb) -> initiate

Boundary (incorrect example; do not imitate):
Original: A fast runner. Bad rewrite: An expeditious runner. The adjective does not fit that ordinary collocation.
Why incorrect: Choose an adjective that collocates with the intended noun and sense.

Tags: advanced_synonym_precision, topic_specific_vocab, substitution, sentence, daily, education, academic, vocab"}, {"id": "en_health_formal_register", "title": "Everyday health language vs formal medical language", "text": "Title: Everyday health language vs formal medical language
When to use: Use for tone in symptom descriptions; this note does not diagnose conditions or recommend care.

Explanation: Preserve the symptom and the speaker in a health-related rewrite. Plain symptom descriptions can already be appropriate. Do not convert everyday uncertainty into a diagnosis or substitute a related medical condition.

Examples:
- I have a very bad headache. -> I have a severe headache.
- She is tired all the time. -> She experiences persistent tiredness.
- My stomach hurts. -> I have stomach pain.
- She's really tired all the time. -> She experiences persistent fatigue.

Boundary (incorrect example; do not imitate):
Original: I feel dizzy. Bad rewrite: I have vertigo. A general symptom does not establish that specific condition.
Why incorrect: Keep the stated symptom; the source does not establish a specific condition.

Tags: formal_register, sentence_transformation, transformation, sentence, health, rewrite"}, {"id": "en_health_phrase_formal", "title": "Informal health phrase vs formal medical phrase", "text": "Title: Informal health phrase vs formal medical phrase
When to use: Use for short symptom expressions; not treatment, emergency triage, or symptom interpretation.

Explanation: Use a clear equivalent for the whole health-related phrase without making a diagnosis. Preserve who reports the experience. A reference for language should not imply clinical authority.

Examples:
- I feel sick to my stomach. -> I feel nauseated.
- I do not feel well. -> I feel unwell.
- My head hurts. -> I have a headache.
- I feel sick to my stomach. -> I am experiencing nausea.

Boundary (incorrect example; do not imitate):
Original: I feel unwell. Bad rewrite: I have an infection. The diagnosis is unsupported.
Why incorrect: Feeling unwell is not evidence for a specific diagnosis.

Tags: phrase_idiom, formal_register, translation, phrase, health"}, {"id": "en_money_vocabulary_precision", "title": "Everyday money word vs precise financial term", "text": "Title: Everyday money word vs precise financial term
When to use: Use for a defined financial vocabulary task; this note is not a complete accounting reference or financial advice.

Explanation: Financial labels require a specified meaning. A broad category and one example of it are not interchangeable in every sentence. Where the prompt is underspecified, explain the missing distinction instead of supplying artificial certainty.

Examples:
- spend less money -> reduce spending
- recover money previously lost -> recoup the money
- an increase in the price -> a price increase
- money earned from sales before expenses (noun) -> revenue

Boundary (incorrect example; do not imitate):
Original: Money was received. Bad rewrite: A profit was earned. Receipts alone do not establish a profit.
Why incorrect: Receipts alone do not establish that revenue exceeded relevant costs.

Tags: advanced_synonym_precision, topic_specific_vocab, substitution, sentence, money, finance, vocab"}, {"id": "en_nominalization", "title": "Verb phrase vs nominalized form", "text": "Title: Verb phrase vs nominalized form
When to use: Use for an explicit verb-to-noun transformation, not as a synonym for passive voice.

Explanation: Nominalization expresses an action through a noun, such as approval or revision. It can help discuss a process as a topic, but often adds words or hides the actor. Preserve the actor when it matters; a noun-based version is not automatically better writing.

Examples:
- The board approved the plan. -> The board gave approval to the plan.
- We revised the schedule. -> We made a revision to the schedule.
- They investigated the error. -> They conducted an investigation into the error.

Boundary (incorrect example; do not imitate):
Original: The board approved it. Bad rewrite: Approval occurred. Responsibility is lost.
Why incorrect: Nominalization should retain the responsible actor when that actor matters.

Tags: formal_register, sentence_transformation, transformation, sentence, work, academic, nominalization"}, {"id": "en_non_restrictive_relative_clause", "title": "Two sentences vs non-restrictive relative clause", "text": "Title: Two sentences vs non-restrictive relative clause
When to use: Use when extra information is parenthetical, not necessary to identify the noun.

Explanation: A non-defining relative clause adds parenthetical information about an already identified referent. Separate an inserted clause with two commas and keep a relative pronoun such as who or which; do not use that. Contrast this with a defining clause that selects a referent.

Examples:
- Asha lives in Leeds. She designed this logo. -> Asha, who designed this logo, lives in Leeds.
- This single invoice is overdue. It arrived on Friday. -> This invoice, which arrived on Friday, is overdue.
- Our only office has reopened. It closed in May. -> Our only office, which closed in May, has reopened.

Boundary (incorrect example; do not imitate):
Bad: Asha, that designed the logo, lives in Leeds. Use who, not that, in this parenthetical clause.
Why incorrect: Parenthetical relative clauses do not allow that as their relative pronoun.

Tags: sentence_transformation, complex_sentence_combination, relative_clause, non_restrictive, transformation, sentence, daily"}, {"id": "en_participle_clause_combination", "title": "Two clauses vs participle clause", "text": "Title: Two clauses vs participle clause
When to use: Use when combining clauses with a participle opener. Do not use for noun-identifying relative clauses.

Explanation: An introductory participle clause normally shares its understood subject with the main clause. Having plus a past participle marks an earlier completed action; an -ing clause may describe simultaneous activity. Check subject and time relations before combining sentences.

Examples:
- Nora checked the address. Then she mailed the form. -> Having checked the address, Nora mailed the form.
- Omar walked home. He listened to a podcast as he walked. -> Walking home, Omar listened to a podcast.
- The students finished the task. Then they left. -> Having finished the task, the students left.
- She studied the data. She reached a conclusion. -> Having studied the data, she reached a conclusion.

Boundary (incorrect example; do not imitate):
Bad: Walking to the office, the rain soaked me. The grammatical subject would be the rain, not the walker.
Why incorrect: The introductory clause needs the walker as the main clause subject.

Tags: sentence_transformation, complex_sentence_combination, participle_clause, transformation, sentence, daily"}, {"id": "en_passive_vs_active_voice", "title": "Active voice vs passive voice", "text": "Title: Active voice vs passive voice
When to use: Use for an explicit active/passive transformation, not a general demand to sound formal.

Explanation: For an ordinary transitive clause, passive be plus a past participle makes the object the subject. Preserve tense, participants, and negation. Choose voice for focus; the passive agent may be omitted when unknown or unneeded, but do not invent an agent when converting back.

Examples:
- Mira checked the invoice. -> The invoice was checked by Mira.
- The parcel was packed by Leo. -> Leo packed the parcel.
- They have not approved the plan. -> The plan has not been approved by them.
- The committee reviewed the proposal. -> The proposal was reviewed by the committee.

Boundary (incorrect example; do not imitate):
Original: Someone opened the door. Bad rewrite: The manager opened the door. The manager was not identified.
Why incorrect: An unspecified agent cannot be replaced with an invented manager.

Tags: sentence_transformation, passive_voice, active_voice, transformation, sentence, work, daily"}, {"id": "en_precise_adjective_choice", "title": "Vague adjective vs precise adjective", "text": "Title: Vague adjective vs precise adjective
When to use: Use for contextual adjective substitutions; a request for formality alone does not establish a new quality.

Explanation: An adjective describes a particular dimension: size, severity, clarity, or importance. Choose the intended dimension from the context rather than replacing every vague adjective with a stronger one.

Examples:
- The instructions are [easy to understand]. -> The instructions are clear.
- The timetable is [not clear]. -> The timetable is unclear.
- The error is [very serious]. -> The error is severe.
- The plan has a [bad] flaw. -> The plan has a critical flaw.

Boundary (incorrect example; do not imitate):
Original: A large building. Bad rewrite: An important building. Size and importance are different dimensions.
Why incorrect: A physical size adjective cannot be replaced with an importance judgment.

Tags: advanced_synonym_precision, substitution, sentence, daily, work, sport"}, {"id": "en_precise_synonym_choice", "title": "General wording vs precise synonym", "text": "Title: General wording vs precise synonym
When to use: Use for a contextual word substitution without a special grammatical transformation; check the whole sentence after inserting the answer.

Explanation: A replacement must fit the word sense, grammar, and surrounding words. Similar dictionary meanings do not guarantee interchangeability. A longer alternative such as utilize is not inherently more precise than use.

Examples:
- The diagram [shows] the process. -> The diagram illustrates the process.
- Please [look at closely] the signature. -> Please examine the signature.
- The meeting will [start] at noon. -> The meeting will begin at noon.
- The project was very [big]. -> The project was very substantial.

Boundary (incorrect example; do not imitate):
Original: She asked a question. Bad rewrite: She solicited a question. The object relationship changes.
Why incorrect: Asking a question and requesting that someone supply a question are different acts.

Tags: advanced_synonym_precision, substitution, sentence, daily, work"}, {"id": "en_relative_clause_combination", "title": "Two sentences vs relative clause", "text": "Title: Two sentences vs relative clause
When to use: Use when extra information selects one referent from several, or the card explicitly requests a defining relative clause.

Explanation: A defining relative clause identifies which person or thing is intended. It normally has no surrounding commas. Use who for people and which or that for things; preserve the noun reference. Choosing defining rather than non-defining changes the information structure.

Examples:
- Several analysts applied. The analyst who speaks Arabic was selected. -> The selected analyst is identified by the clause who speaks Arabic.
- Choose the file. It contains the final figures. -> Choose the file that contains the final figures.
- I need the tool. It opens this panel. -> I need the tool that opens this panel.
- The manager approved the budget. She leads the project. -> The manager who leads the project approved the budget.

Boundary (incorrect example; do not imitate):
If there is only one already identified sister, adding identifying information without commas may imply a different context.
Why incorrect: Defining and parenthetical clauses assume different identification contexts.

Tags: sentence_transformation, complex_sentence_combination, relative_clause, transformation, sentence, daily"}, {"id": "en_science_formal_register", "title": "Casual observation vs formal scientific description", "text": "Title: Casual observation vs formal scientific description
When to use: Use for experimental observations and research reports, not for a general request to define a scientific term.

Explanation: Report observations and interpretations separately. A rewrite must not invent statistical tests, significance, mechanisms, or support for a hypothesis. Active voice and first person may be appropriate; follow the relevant publication or course convention.

Examples:
- We noticed an unexpected change. -> We observed an unexpected change.
- The test ran as planned. -> The test proceeded as planned.
- We do not know why the signal changed. -> The reason for the signal change remains unknown.
- The experiment worked. -> The experiment functioned as intended.

Boundary (incorrect example; do not imitate):
Original: Scores improved. Bad rewrite: Scores improved significantly. Statistical significance was not established.
Why incorrect: Do not imply a statistical result without a stated test and evidence.

Tags: formal_register, sentence_transformation, transformation, sentence, science, academic, rewrite"}, {"id": "en_single_precise_verb", "title": "Loose phrase vs single precise verb", "text": "Title: Loose phrase vs single precise verb
When to use: Use when a card explicitly requests a single verb, before applying generic synonym or register guidance.

Explanation: Replace a phrase with one verb only when it expresses the same action and takes compatible objects and prepositions. Preserve tense and agent. Concision does not license inventing successful outcomes.

Examples:
- They [talked about] the timetable. -> They discussed the timetable.
- She [made improvements to] the draft. -> She improved the draft.
- We [gave an explanation of] the rule. -> We explained the rule.
- He [talked about] the risks at length. -> He addressed the risks at length.

Boundary (incorrect example; do not imitate):
Original: They tried to repair it. Bad rewrite: They repaired it. Attempt and success are different.
Why incorrect: A repair attempt does not imply a successful repair.

Tags: single_precise_verb, advanced_synonym_precision, substitution, sentence, work, sport, tech, daily"}, {"id": "en_sport_formal_sentence", "title": "Casual sport report vs formal sport reporting language", "text": "Title: Casual sport report vs formal sport reporting language
When to use: Use for full sentences about sporting performance rather than short predictions or sport terminology.

Explanation: Report an athletic performance with the same level of detail and certainty as the source. Clear journalistic prose need not add composure, teamwork, or records when they were not described.

Examples:
- She played very well under pressure. -> She performed very well under pressure.
- The team won by three points. -> The team secured a three-point victory.
- The players made several mistakes. -> The players made several errors.
- She played really well under pressure. -> She performed very well under pressure.

Boundary (incorrect example; do not imitate):
Original: The player performed well. Bad rewrite: The player broke the league record. The achievement is unsupported.
Why incorrect: A record requires comparison evidence, not a general positive assessment.

Tags: formal_register, sentence_transformation, transformation, sentence, sport, rewrite"}, {"id": "en_sport_phrase_formal", "title": "Informal sport phrase vs formal sports commentary phrase", "text": "Title: Informal sport phrase vs formal sports commentary phrase
When to use: Use for phrase-level sport reporting; use sport sentence guidance for a full performance description.

Explanation: Rephrase a short sporting expression while retaining the prediction, result, and confidence level. A professional report need not exaggerate athletic performance.

Examples:
- They may win. -> Victory is possible for them.
- They are likely to lose. -> They are expected to lose.
- The match is over. -> The match has ended.
- They're going to lose. -> They are expected to lose.

Boundary (incorrect example; do not imitate):
Original: They may win. Bad rewrite: They will win. A possibility became a certainty.
Why incorrect: May expresses possibility; will asserts a predicted outcome more strongly.

Tags: phrase_idiom, formal_register, translation, phrase, sport"}, {"id": "en_sport_vocabulary_precision", "title": "Generic sport description vs precise sports term", "text": "Title: Generic sport description vs precise sports term
When to use: Use for contextual sport vocabulary, not an unsupported claim about a score or achievement.

Explanation: Choose a sporting expression only when its meaning is supplied by the task. Admission of defeat, loss of a match, and conceding a goal are different events. Do not infer a record from a general description of good performance.

Examples:
- a session for practicing a sport -> a training session
- admit defeat in a contest -> concede defeat
- the points recorded for each side -> the score
- win (verb) -> triumph

Boundary (incorrect example; do not imitate):
Original: The runner did well. Bad rewrite: The runner set a personal best. No record comparison was given.
Why incorrect: Good performance does not establish a personal record.

Tags: advanced_synonym_precision, topic_specific_vocab, substitution, sentence, sport, vocab"}, {"id": "en_tech_vocabulary_precision", "title": "Generic description vs precise technical term", "text": "Title: Generic description vs precise technical term
When to use: Use for software-operation vocabulary with enough context; do not infer a root cause from an outage.

Explanation: Use technical terms according to the described operation. Testing, reviewing, deploying, and optimizing are not interchangeable improvements in formality. Preserve whether the source states an action, outcome, or symptom.

Examples:
- The process stopped unexpectedly. -> The process terminated unexpectedly.
- We need to fix the defect. -> We need to resolve the defect.
- Make execution faster. -> Improve execution speed.
- The app [crashed]. -> The app terminated unexpectedly.

Boundary (incorrect example; do not imitate):
Original: The program was implemented. Bad rewrite: The program was deployed. Implementation does not entail release.
Why incorrect: Building software and releasing it are different lifecycle events.

Tags: advanced_synonym_precision, topic_specific_vocab, substitution, sentence, tech, vocab"}, {"id": "en_work_formal_register", "title": "Casual workplace language vs formal business language", "text": "Title: Casual workplace language vs formal business language
When to use: Use for workplace sentence rewrites such as target reports and email openings; use the phrase note for short interaction formulas.

Explanation: For workplace reports, make the actor, action, and limits of the claim clear. Choose professional wording without implying that all business writing must be impersonal. Retain hedging where the speaker is uncertain.

Examples:
- We did not hit the target. -> We did not meet the target.
- I am checking on the request. -> I am following up on the request.
- She runs the branch. -> She manages the branch.
- We didn't hit our targets this quarter. -> We did not meet our targets this quarter.

Boundary (incorrect example; do not imitate):
Original: We think the delay is temporary. Bad rewrite: The delay is temporary. The confidence changed.
Why incorrect: Removing we think strengthens the level of certainty.

Tags: formal_register, sentence_transformation, transformation, sentence, work, rewrite"}, {"id": "en_work_phrase_formal", "title": "Informal work phrase vs formal workplace alternative", "text": "Title: Informal work phrase vs formal workplace alternative
When to use: Use for short workplace interaction phrases; use the workplace sentence note for reports of organizational facts.

Explanation: Preserve the intent of workplace interaction: follow up, request a response, close a meeting, or acknowledge an idea. Politeness does not require a long formula. Keep urgency only when originally stated.

Examples:
- Let us finish the meeting. -> Let us bring the meeting to a close.
- Please reply about the schedule. -> Please respond regarding the schedule.
- That is a useful suggestion. -> That is a useful proposal.
- That's a great idea. -> That is an excellent idea.

Boundary (incorrect example; do not imitate):
Original: Please reply when you can. Bad rewrite: Respond today. The deadline and politeness changed.
Why incorrect: Preserve the flexible timing and the original request tone.

Tags: phrase_idiom, formal_register, translation, phrase, work"}, {"id": "en_work_vocabulary_precision", "title": "Everyday work word vs precise business term", "text": "Title: Everyday work word vs precise business term
When to use: Use for workplace vocabulary with a defined action or purpose, not general email tone.

Explanation: Professional terms may name different activities rather than stronger synonyms. A consultation seeks advice; not every meeting does. State the context needed for the target term and preserve participants.

Examples:
- work together on a task -> collaborate on a task
- a meeting to seek advice -> a consultation
- leave a project voluntarily -> withdraw from a project
- meeting to seek professional advice (noun) -> consultation

Boundary (incorrect example; do not imitate):
Original: A meeting occurred. Bad rewrite: A consultation occurred. The purpose of the meeting was not stated.
Why incorrect: A consultation implies an advice-seeking purpose absent from a generic meeting.

Tags: advanced_synonym_precision, topic_specific_vocab, substitution, sentence, work, vocab"}]}

jobs.question: Does receiving money necessarily mean earning a profit?

references.title: Casual money phrase vs formal financial phrase
references.text:
Title: Casual money phrase vs formal financial phrase
When to use: Use for informal financial phrases; use the sentence note for full reports and the vocabulary note for defined terms.

Explanation: Restate a short money-related expression without inserting a cause or a new accounting measure. If the informal phrase is ambiguous, ask what it refers to before choosing a specialized term.

Examples:
- We are losing money. -> We are making a financial loss.
- We need to spend less. -> We need to reduce spending.
- The price has gone up. -> The price has increased.
- We're in the red. -> The organization is operating at a deficit.

Boundary (incorrect example; do not imitate):
Original: Money came in. Bad rewrite: Profit increased. Receipts alone do not establish profit.
Why incorrect: Money received and profit are different quantities.

Tags: phrase_idiom, formal_register, translation, phrase, money, finance
